# Objective

The objective of this Coursework Project is to analyse and model the relationship between measurements and PCR outcomes. This project requires the clear demonstration and mathematical usage of:

- Linear Algebra
- Probability and Maximum Likelihood
- Optimisation
- Geometric Classification

The components required to complete the objective was the following:

1. Exploratory Linear Algebra

Covariance Analysis, Eigenvalues/Eigenvectors or rank analysis, Brief Geometric Interpretation.

1. Logistic Regression

Mathematical Formulation, Log-Likelihood Derivation, Optimisation Via Gradient Descent.

1. K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN)

Distance-Based Classification, Discussion of Metric Choice.

1. Support Vector Machine (SVM)

Margin Interpretation, Explanation of Optimisation Objective, Use of Linear SVM.

1. Comparative Analysis

Compare the Above Three Approaches, Interpret differences mathematically.

# Report

## Introduction

This report's goal is to analyse the dataset provided and model any potential relationship between measurements and PCR outcomes to attempt to display a correlation that may exist between Data and Outcome.

Our data contains the Haematological, Biochemical, and Immunological data from patients who underwent the PCR test, and using such information to predict whether said patient will test Positive or Negative for a particular illness. This dataset is potentially linked to COVID-19 PCR testing (not explicitly stated, only hinted), which, the outcomes of said model, if deemed reliable enough, may result in it not only being used more widely, but also having the model altered to test for different illnesses (Such as HPV, HIV, Tuberculosis, or any other pathogenic illness) in the future.

### 1.1 Brief Plan

The plan of action with this report is to briefly explain the mathematics behind what I've used, the outcome at which said maths would achieve (as shown through the accompanying .ipynb file), and what each result means for the data.

Our data was cleaned of any potential NA entries, which did not exist in the given dataset analysed.

Our data is severely unbalanced with a 91-9 ratio split (91% being negative "0", 9% being positive "1") and as such, during our analysis of this data, we reweight our data to try and equally represent both sides.

### 2.3 K-Nearest Neighbours

K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN) [\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-nearest_neighbors_algorithm) is a non-parametric supervised learning method used as a classification (and sometimes regression) algorithm. During the testing phase, the algorithm computes the distance between the test point and all training points, selects the k closest neighbours, and will then predict the class of said points through a majority vote (If more of a particular classification exist in a given distance around the test point compared to another, then said point will be assigned the majority classification).

To calculate the distance between points, we use Euclidean Distance formula for this.

Let:

Training Point.

Distance.

As we have 37 features in our dataset, we can't just use a simple x, y, we must use a 37-Dimensional Vector instead, which changes our Distance formula into the following:

All 37 features are continuous, numeric measurements, standardised during preprocessing (Mean = 0, Variance = 1), and the Euclidean Distance is just measuring the geometric proximity between the test and training points, treating all dimensions equally.

We tested from 1 to 20 k-values and used our KNN algorithm to assess the accuracy of each k-value to find the most accurate within our given range.![](data:image/png;base64,)  
From this, between K values 1 to 4, our accuracy remained about the same (roughly 95.6%), K = 6 accuracy was lower than our first 4 (at about 95.2%) , and beyond K = 7, we see a trend of accuracy decreasing, leaving us with our best result found at K = 5, as it gives an accuracy rating of around 96.3%, the highest accuracy value found.

Viewing our Classification Report for this:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

From this classification report, we can see that we have a 97% in precision when it comes to detecting negative results, and a 99% in recall, so about 1% of our actual negatives will be misclassified as positive results.

For positives, we have an 89% in precision in detecting positive results, and a 68% in recall, so 32% of our actual positives, will be misclassified as negative results.

Unlike our Logistic Regression model, KNN has no class weighting needs. The majority voting system favours the negative class (as its unbalanced in its favour), resulting in higher overall accuracy (as denoted by our k = 5 accuracy), but a lower recall for positive cases.

This means that KNN will miss 32% of the true positives. When dealing with a potentially life-threatening illness, such high levels of false negatives may result in a significant number of deaths occurring because of delayed or no medical care.

### 2.4 Support Vector Machine

Support Vector Machines (SVMs) [\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Support_vector_machine) are a supervised max-margin model with associated learning algorithms that analyse data for classification and regression analysis. The goal of SVM is to maximise the margin between the two classes, the larger the margin, the better the model performs on new and unseen data.

However, its low precision for positives (49%) will result in many false positives, which, in practice, for roughly one positively identified patient, there was a false positive, and on a larger scale, will begin to find more false positives than true positives. This would greatly increase the wait time in real life due to the number of multiple screenings that'll take place, potentially causing a similar outcome to if said patients who were truly positive, were falsely identified as negative, increasing the medical care wait time. Even if it correctly recalls 87% of these cases, such a low precision score could make the usage of this algorithm untenable.

### 2.5 Comparative Analysis

Here, I will be making the final comparison and suggestion for which model should be used within this situation, between Logistic Regression, K-Nearest Neighbours, and Support Vector Machine.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Comparing each Model:

Their objective functions:

The Logistic Regression model aims to minimise the negative log-likelihood to maximize the probability of correct predictions through adjusting weights, it prioritises getting the positive classifications correct over negative classification.

KNN just measures the distance a point has with the other trained data points, and predicts the result through proximity voting, where the more that are close to an unclassified point, results in said point being classified as the majority.

SVM desires to maximise the margin through minimising the magnitude of the weight vector, it attempts to find the optimal hyperplane that splits both results. It reweights to balance the severely unbalanced data.

Putting this into the context of PCR testing for a new illness that is highly infectious, we should compare all our models on the statement of "What model is most likely to correctly identify a true positive, whilst minimising the false negatives."

For Logistic Regression, it has a recall of 100%, meaning that it theoretically should always detect a true positive, however, it isn't that precise at 32%, meaning that out of 100 people flagged positive, 68 would be a false positive, but it would always detect those 32, and be correct about it.

For K-Nearest Neighbours, it has a recall of 68%, with only 89% precision. Out of 100 people, on average, KNN may find about 32 of its truly positive individuals, classified as negative (false negative). However, for all its predicted positives, 89% are truly infected, with only a 11% being a false positive reading.

For SVM, it has an 87% recall, with a 49% in precision, out of 100 people, on average, it misses 13 of those infected, with a false positive rate at 51%.

In my judgement, it's far better to detect all that are truly infected, or had an ailment, with many false positives which can be double screened to rule out, as at most, its only inconveniencing them, and if it's not in such a supermajority (if it marked 100 as positive but only 5 are positive truly), it's a lot more useful to have, especially compared to those who will dish out false negatives.

And with that, the Logistic Regression Model is the best choice for this situation, it is better to detect all that are infected with false positives that are, at most, an inconvenience, over potentially condemning several patients to death due to them being a false negative, all parties that require medical attention can receive it.

This is even more in Logistic Regressions favour, as if what you are testing for was some infectious disease, every false negative is potentially another group of people being infected. Or even if testing for cancer, it's better to find all those who had it, and have inconvenienced people, than risk having more die due to a false negative.
